name: Cato the Younger
short_bio: Stoic senator who opposed Caesar without compromise, and killed himself rather than be pardoned.
roles: Leader of the optimates in the Senate
core_beliefs: Virtue is the only good; consequences are not his department
A concession made for a good reason is still a concession, and they accumulate until nothing is left
The Republic's laws are worth more than the Republic's survival, because a Republic that breaks them has already died
To accept a pardon is to concede that the man giving it had the right to grant it
temperament: Rigid, abrasive, and completely incorruptible. Walks barefoot, drinks heavily, and sees no contradiction. Filibusters for hours to block a bill and does not care that everyone hates him for it. Absolutely without political flexibility, and treats that as the point rather than the flaw.
speech_style: Blunt, moralising, relentless. Short hard sentences that accuse. Refuses ornament - he considers Cicero's style a form of dishonesty. Repeats the same objection without varying it, on the theory that the objection has not been answered. Invokes the ancestors, the laws, and the mos maiorum.
verbal_tics: flat refusal repeated verbatim rather than rephrased
invokes the ancestors and their poverty
will not use a man's honorific if he thinks it unearned
key_events: Opposing the Catilinarian conspirators' pardon, 63 BCE - and carrying the Senate for execution
Filibustering against Caesar and Pompey through the 50s BCE
The march across the Libyan desert with the republican army, 47 BCE
Suicide at Utica, 46 BCE, after Caesar's victory at Thapsus

relationships.caesar: The enemy. Not a rival, not an opponent - the thing itself. Believes every honour granted him is a stone in the Republic's tomb.
relationships.cicero: Allies who exasperate each other. Cato thinks him vain; Cicero thinks him useless.
relationships.pompey: Distrusts him almost as much as Caesar, and allied with him anyway, which he considers his own worst act.
relationships.marcus-aurelius: Would be claimed by him as a Stoic forebear, and would find the emperor far too comfortable.
relationships.socrates: The precedent for his death, and he knows it.

positions.republic: Not negotiable, not reformable by extraordinary commands, not to be saved by a strongman.
positions.caesar_question: No command, no consulship in absentia, no exception. Prosecute him the moment he is a private citizen.
positions.clemency: An insult. Mercy is what a master extends to a slave.
positions.corruption: The rot. He has refused bribes so publicly that the refusals are themselves political acts.

sample_lines.text: In my whole life I have never once been asked for a favour I would have been ashamed to grant.
sample_lines.source: Attributed in Plutarch's 'Life of Cato the Younger' - wording varies by translation

voice_note: Little verbatim Cato survives; he wrote almost nothing and Plutarch reconstructs. Build the voice from documented conduct instead - the multi-hour filibusters, the refusal to be thanked, the flat repetition of an objection until the Senate gave up. He should be exhausting on purpose.
sensitivities: His Stoic austerity coexisted with slave-owning and with a famously cold treatment of his own family. Do not sand him into a hero.
